source.title: Trained on 100 million words and still in shape: BERT meets British National Corpus
source.authors: David Samuel; Andrey Kutuzov; Lilja Øvrelid; Erik Velldal

record.tranche_reason: The study varies the number of training steps and reports downstream performance, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy or perform a parameter/data/compute scaling-law fit.
record.gate_note: The study does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, a sweep over model parameter counts, power-law fits or extrapolations, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its architecture comparisons report downstream and linguistic benchmarks, not loss, so they do not test V4 as stated. The relevant results are its reported downstream performance under different training-step counts. Cited scaling results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: A three-point sweep of pre-training steps (1/4×, 1/2×, 1×, 2×) on one 98M-parameter LTG-BERT model, trained on the 100M-word BNC and seen hundreds of times, reports downstream scores. This bears weakly on V6 (downstream gains with more compute) in a heavily repeated-data setting. There is no loss measurement, no size sweep and no fit, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. On steps, the authors say 2× gives no noticeable gain, 1/2× is comparable and 1/4× degrades, calling current methods sampling-inefficient. The paper's main conclusions are different, though. 100M curated BNC words suffice to outperform original BERT-base, NSP does not help, span masking beats subword masking, and huge data is not always necessary.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fit held-out-loss scaling laws across model sizes, tokens and compute, the study varies training steps for a fixed-size BERT-like model and evaluates downstream benchmarks.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream performance changes with the number of training steps: the 1/4-step run degrades, while the 1/2-step run is described as comparable to the default.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed ~98M parameters, architecture and training choices change MNLI by up to −1.4 and BLiMP by up to −0.9 (Table 2). Examples: pre-norm vs NormFormer, absolute positional embeddings, weight decay 0.01. These are measured downstream, not as loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, normalization placement and training hyperparameters shift downstream and BLiMP scores of small masked LMs by about 1 point.

fits_no_version.finding: A curated 100M-word BNC beats a random 100M Wikipedia+BookCorpus subset downstream (GLUE avg 88.2 vs 87.8; HANS 64.4 vs 62.5; BLiMP 83.4 vs 82.0).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed token budget, data quality changes downstream performance of masked LMs.

record.problems: The relevant scaling-related evidence covers only one base-sized model, one corpus and a small set of training-step settings. The reported outcomes are downstream benchmarks rather than held-out pretraining loss, and the study does not fit a scaling curve.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows were left out. Results comparing architecture and training configurations, masking objectives, NSP objectives, and corpus choice are not rows for the versions tested here because they do not measure the claim’s stated loss scaling or its downstream scale/loss relationship.

untested.parts: Predictability of downstream performance across model sizes or from pretraining loss. Behaviour with fresh (non-repeated) data. Any fitted trend; only four step settings on one model.
No held-out pretraining loss is reported and there are no parameter, token or compute sweeps.
Architecture ablations at fixed size use downstream and BLiMP scores, not loss.
Repeated data is present, but no loss or power-law form is reported.

missing.what: Per-setting numeric scores for the step sweep across GLUE tasks, HANS, edge probing and BLiMP. The rows carry only the qualitative text.

record.verdict_notes: r3 was marked reversed, but its direction matches V6. The record's 'challenges' label is too strong, so it is replaced by limits_scope. The data-repetition regime (every token seen ≥250 times) means data is the bottleneck, which may explain the plateau. This is weak evidence on V6 given one model and four step settings. Hoffmann et al. is cited only.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute; power-law behaviour over several orders of magnitude.
Fitting power laws on small runs and predicting losses of much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations across compute budgets.
Whether architecture differences change held-out loss only slightly at fixed parameter count; architecture comparisons here use other evaluation measures.
Power-law behaviour in other modalities or training regimes.
The study varies training steps for one model and reports benchmark performance, but does not test downstream predictability across model sizes or against pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: LTG-BERT (subword masking)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of pre-training steps to 2× the default.
rows.value: Increasing the steps two times does not lead to a noticeably better performance.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this qualitative comparison
rows.note: The paper gives this comparison as an explicit qualitative summary of its downstream results.
rows.check: Value should carry Table 3 numbers. Against the default, GLUE avg moves 88.2→88.6, HANS 64.4→65.3, edge probing 95.3→95.3 and BLiMP 83.4→83.5. All are within about 1 sd, and the authors call it not noticeably better. State absent is right.

rows.subject: LTG-BERT (subword masking)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of pre-training steps to 1/2 the default.
rows.value: Training for half the time is enough to get comparable performance.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this qualitative comparison
rows.note: The paper summarizes the downstream results as comparable to the default-step run.
rows.check: Halving steps gives GLUE avg 88.5, HANS 62.4 (−2.0), edge 95.2 and BLiMP 83.5, against the default 88.2/64.4/95.3/83.4. Only HANS drops clearly, so this is a small effect in V6's direction rather than absent. Add the numbers.

rows.subject: LTG-BERT (subword masking)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of pre-training steps to 1/4 the default.
rows.value: Decreasing the training steps further starts to degrade the downstream results too much.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this qualitative comparison
rows.note: The paper also states that with 1/4 of the default steps, every BNC token is seen roughly 250 times during training.
rows.check: Mislabelled as reversed. Fewer steps giving worse results (GLUE avg 87.5, HANS 58.6, edge 95.0, BLiMP 83.2) is the direction V6 predicts: more compute, better downstream. Baseline should also be stated with numbers.

relationships.condition: 98M LTG-BERT, subword MLM, BNC 100M words repeated ~250–2000 times, steps varied 1/4× to 2×
relationships.reason: Downstream rises with steps only up to about 1/2× and then plateaus: 2× is within noise of the default (r1). Quartering steps degrades results (r3), and halving costs only HANS (r2). Gains saturate under heavy data repetition.
relationships.display_finding: Gains largely plateaued around half the default training steps: doubling steps stayed within noise, quartering degraded results, and halving hurt only HANS.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: LTG-BERT with subword masking on BNC, varying pre-training steps
reader_labels.reason: The tested step changes do not show a consistent downstream improvement with more training: 2× is not noticeably better and 1/2× is comparable, while 1/4× degrades; see r1–r3.
